label: Memory
learning_takeaway: Distinguish encoding, retaining and recovering information rather than treating memory as a recording.
support_note: The source identifies three functions of the memory system.

label: Working memory model
learning_takeaway: Explore a model that separates temporary verbal and visual-spatial processing under executive control.
support_note: The passage names limited-capacity subsystems and a central executive.

label: Sensory memory
learning_takeaway: Distinguish very brief sensory persistence from longer-term storage.
support_note: The section describes brief storage within the Atkinson–Shiffrin model.

label: Self-reference effect
learning_takeaway: Investigate why relating information to oneself can improve later remembering.
support_note: The passage defines a relative memory advantage for personally relevant material.

label: Procedural memory
learning_takeaway: Distinguish remembering how to perform a skill from verbally recalling its instructions.
support_note: Riding and driving illustrate skilled actions without fully reportable knowledge.

label: Proactive interference
learning_takeaway: Understand how an older memory can obstruct recall of newly learned information.
support_note: An old phone number interfering with a new one illustrates the direction.

label: Retroactive interference
learning_takeaway: Understand how later learning can obstruct access to older information.
support_note: The section explicitly contrasts its direction with proactive interference.

label: Source misattribution
learning_takeaway: Recognize a remembered detail whose origin has been confused.
support_note: Misattribution concerns the source of remembered information, not necessarily its content.

label: Misinformation effect
learning_takeaway: Explore how misleading information after an event can alter later reports.
support_note: Loftus and Palmer's wording manipulation supplies a bounded experimental example.

label: Henry Molaison
learning_takeaway: Compare impaired new declarative memories with preserved improvement on practiced tasks.
support_note: The H. M. example describes repeated introductions and improving puzzle performance.

label: Absolute sensory threshold
learning_takeaway: Interpret detection threshold as a probability under controlled conditions.
support_note: The criterion is detection on half the presentations, not an absolute sensory boundary.

label: Just-noticeable difference
learning_takeaway: See why noticing a change depends on the starting stimulus intensity.
support_note: The light example and Weber discussion distinguish difference from absolute thresholds.

label: Sensory adaptation
learning_takeaway: Distinguish continuing sensory stimulation from reduced conscious notice over time.
support_note: The section contrasts sensation with perception during prolonged stimulation.

label: Inattentional blindness
learning_takeaway: Understand how a visible unexpected event can escape notice during another task.
support_note: The basketball-counting experiment grounds a qualified attention-dependent failure.

label: Signal detection theory
learning_takeaway: Explore detecting a target among noise when expectations and task goals influence reports.
support_note: The paragraph describes meaningful signals amid distracting background stimulation.

label: Figure–ground organization
learning_takeaway: See why a single image can reverse between an object and its background.
support_note: The vase-versus-faces example illustrates alternative visual segmentation.

label: Perceptual closure
learning_takeaway: Explore how incomplete parts can be perceived as a complete object.
support_note: The source distinguishes completion from a collection of separate parts.

label: Good continuation
learning_takeaway: Understand why smooth continuations are often grouped rather than broken alternatives.
support_note: The passage describes a preference for continuous smoothly flowing lines.

label: Mental set
learning_takeaway: Recognize persistence with a formerly useful approach after circumstances change.
support_note: The definition distinguishes habitual strategy from the present problem's demands.

label: Functional fixedness
learning_takeaway: See how an object's conventional use can hide an alternative solution.
support_note: Duncker's materials and the candle task exemplify restricted use assumptions.

label: Anchoring bias
learning_takeaway: Investigate how an initial focal value can steer subsequent judgment.
support_note: The housing-budget example illustrates disproportionate focus on one information point.

label: Confirmation bias
learning_takeaway: Recognize selective attention to information supporting an existing belief.
support_note: The section contrasts noticed confirming episodes with ignored counterexamples.

label: Hindsight bias
learning_takeaway: Distinguish knowing an outcome from having predicted it beforehand.
support_note: The passage defines the retrospective impression that an event was predictable.

label: Availability heuristic
learning_takeaway: Explore how accessible examples substitute for broader evidence in judgment.
support_note: The text notes that an available precedent may poorly inform the decision.

label: Intrinsic motivation
learning_takeaway: Distinguish doing an activity for satisfaction from doing it for an external reward.
support_note: The opening contrasts sources of motivation while allowing mixtures.

label: Overjustification effect
learning_takeaway: Examine when expected external rewards can reduce interest in an enjoyable activity.
support_note: The text qualifies effects by tangible versus verbal rewards and expectation.

label: Yerkes–Dodson relationship
learning_takeaway: Investigate why task difficulty matters when relating arousal to performance.
support_note: The chapter explicitly rejects one universally optimal middle arousal level.

label: Self-efficacy
learning_takeaway: Distinguish believing one can complete a task from valuing its reward.
support_note: Bandura's theory links capability beliefs with motivated action.

label: Cognitive dissonance
learning_takeaway: Explore responses to discomfort when commitments and behavior conflict.
support_note: The source describes changing beliefs or behavior to reduce inconsistency.

label: Elaboration likelihood model
learning_takeaway: Compare evaluating an argument with responding to peripheral cues.
support_note: The model distinguishes effortful message evaluation from endorsement or affective cues.

label: Foot-in-the-door technique
learning_takeaway: Explore the qualified finding that a small request can precede increased agreement to a larger one.
support_note: Freedman and Fraser's sign study supplies the specific experimental comparison.

label: Asch's conformity experiments
learning_takeaway: Examine public agreement with a clearly mistaken majority in a particular experimental setting.
support_note: Confederate answers, dissent and public responding are described; later variability is acknowledged.

label: Normative social influence
locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
learning_takeaway: Distinguish joining a group to gain acceptance from believing its answer is correct.
support_note: The source links normative conformity with fitting in and avoiding ridicule.

label: Informational social influence
locator: Why conform? normative versus informational influence
learning_takeaway: Understand relying on others as information when a situation is ambiguous.
support_note: The smoke-in-a-theater example illustrates uncertainty-driven conformity.

label: Milgram's obedience experiments
learning_takeaway: Compare obedience in the original setup with changes produced by proximity and setting.
support_note: Participants believed shocks were real; the text describes situation-dependent variation.

label: Psychology
learning_takeaway: Understand how observable behavior and reports support inferences about mental processes.
support_note: The definition and empirical-method discussion support a broad-field control.

label: Inter-rater reliability
learning_takeaway: Check whether different observers classify the same behavior consistently.
support_note: The source defines agreement between independent observers as a reliability type.

label: Test–retest reliability
learning_takeaway: Distinguish stability across repeated measurements from agreement among observers.
support_note: The passage defines consistency across multiple administrations.

label: Construct validity
learning_takeaway: Ask whether an operational measure captures the intended psychological concept.
support_note: Consistency alone is explicitly distinguished from measuring the intended attribute.

label: Ecological validity
learning_takeaway: Assess how closely a research setting represents real-world behavior.
support_note: Naturalistic observation's realism is weighed against loss of experimental control.

label: Experimenter expectancy bias
learning_takeaway: Understand how a researcher's expectations can shape interpretation of ambiguous responses.
support_note: The test-scoring example motivates concealment of group assignments.

label: Double-blind study
learning_takeaway: Compare controlling participant expectations with controlling researcher expectations.
support_note: The definition conceals assignment from both participants and researchers.

label: Research debriefing
learning_takeaway: Understand why concealed research purposes must be explained after deceptive studies.
support_note: The paragraph specifies purpose, data use and reasons for deception.

label: Deception in psychological research
learning_takeaway: Examine the tension between realistic responses and participants' knowledge of a study's purpose.
support_note: The source explains avoiding response distortion while requiring ethical limits and debriefing.

label: Social desirability bias
learning_takeaway: Consider why answers about behavior may reflect a wish to appear acceptable.
support_note: Survey respondents may underreport drinking or conceal attitudes to look good.
